::: {.cell .markdown id="0uYyVKx1V0o0"}
##Data normalization Data is typically normalized before to be fed to
Machine Learning models. An example is the Z-scoring normalization.

    mu = X_train.mean(0)
    sig = X_train.std(0)

    X_train -= mu
    X_train /= sig

    X_val -= mu
    X_val /= sig

    X_test -= mu
    X_test /= sig

This is implemented in the
[StandardScaler](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.StandardScaler.html)
class. Alternatively, we use the
[RobustScaler](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.preprocessing.RobustScaler.html)
class if we suppose that outliers may be in the training data. This
computes robust training data statistics (e.g., median instead of mean).
:::

::: {.cell .markdown id="xPNZw7U82xmc"}
#The (K-) Nearest Neighbor classifier (kNN)

We use the kNN classifier, however for the purpose of this exercise, any
classifier can be used as a black box. It is the simplest machine
learning classifier. The key idea behind this classifier is to classify
a new sample according to its closest training sample.

Each time we have to classify a new sample, we compute its distance from
training samples and take the minimum. The predicted class of the new
sample will be the class of the closest training sample.

More generarly, the K-NN considers K (3 in the figure) closest training
samples. The predicted class of the new sample will be the result of the
majority vote of the K nearest training sample classes.

![image.png](data:image/png;base64,)

The NN classifier **does not learn a model**. A real **training phase is
not performed**.
:::
